newsitem.title: USA: Despite progress Peru still faces many challenges.
newsitem.headline: Despite progress Peru still faces many challenges.

text.p: Although Peru has made enormous progress in fighting both hyper-inflation and terrorism, U.S. and Peruvian experts said the country still faces many challenges in generating sustainable economic growth.

Speaking to a meeting sponsored by the Americas Society, Albert Fishlow, senior fellow for economics at the Council for Foreign Relations said: "I think the real question is not the continuity of the current policies, or the commitment to lower rates of inflation and lower deficits...I think the fundamental problems are lower rates of growth."

While Fishlow recognizes the importance of the tremendous changes that have taken place in Peru over the last seven years, internal domestic savings were still inadequate to bolster the country's economic growth.
"Peru has the problem, which is characteristic of every country in the region, with the exception of Chile," he said.

"Internal domestic savings are inadequate to support a necessary rate of growth and, in the absence of that, one sees Latin America going back to a structure...that it has had historically, which is dependence upon external savings and upon external participation in the economy."
Another economic challenge Peru faces in the short-term is its current account deficit.

"You are going to see that...the current account deficit is going to be much larger than currently estimated and how the markets register that, I dont know what the answer" will be, said Roberto Danino, partner at Washington D.C.-based William, Cutler & Pickering.
In regard to the hostage situation at the Japanese Embassy in Lima, Danino said: "I think the market has factored in the situation as is, but the market has not factored in the variety of outcomes."
Over the longer term, experts said Peru needs to take further steps in reforming both the judiciary and the country's political system.

"One major reform that still needs to be addressed...is the judiciary. I think if you want an open market system...you have to have an effective" independent jury service that enforces property rights, said Danino.
Fishlow expressed some doubt and concern about the future of politics in Peru.

"It would be tragic for Peru were President Fujimori to continue in power after the year 2000. It would be an indication of a lack of continuity and the lack of ability to pass along a process that had to be continued by others...and in the absence of a structure and mechanism for generating that political capability, one must be concerned," he said.
